bridges.mechanism: A rise in offensive strikes targeting shipping, ports, and regional infrastructure in the Gulf rapidly disrupts logistics and energy supplies (and damages intermediate suppliers), causing semiconductor fabs and their supply chains to miss inputs or shipments and reducing effective production throughput.

A higher tempo of offensive strikes in the theater increases the number of direct attacks on commercial vessels, mines laid, and near-miss incidents as combatants and proxies target or mistake shipping, raising maritime security incidents.

A rise in initiated offensive strikes produces sudden risk shocks and news-driven repricing across fixed-income markets, increasing intraday and realized volatility as investors rapidly reassess sovereign and term premia.

A sharper tempo of retaliatory strikes raises regional and global risk premia and sanctions‑compliance concerns, prompting institutional investors and banks to pull back or delay funding for geopolitically exposed AI projects and reducing near‑term capital flows into the AI sector.

An increased rate of retaliatory strikes raising the likelihood of hits on export terminals, loading infrastructure, or tankers directly reduces export operations and forces cancellations or suspensions of seaborne hydrocarbon shipments.

A rise in Iran's retaliatory-strike tempo signals/reflects increased operational activity and willingness to employ or export munitions and tactical systems (e.g., armed UAVs, missiles) that Iran can transfer to Russia, enabling Moscow to increase strike rates in Ukraine.

Escalating diplomatic hostility in the US–Iran confrontation prompts policymakers to expand export controls, sanctions and secondary‑sanctions enforcement and to coordinate allied tech‑security measures, directly increasing geopolitical friction centered on technology between the US and other major tech actors (notably China).
Escalating diplomatic hostility and public threats increase trader, insurer, and investor perception of disruption risk, prompting higher risk premia and precautionary market behaviour.

Higher diplomatic tensions provoke capital flight and exchange‑rate stress in exposed or regional currencies, prompting official authorities to increase FX intervention (selling FX reserves or buying domestic currency) to defend rates.

A sustained increase in deployed military assets drives accelerated defense procurement of high‑end servers, accelerators and hardened compute for ISR and operational AI, drawing from constrained global inventories and temporarily reducing civilian deployable compute capacity.

Larger deployed naval and interdiction forces in and around chokepoints lead to enforced inspections, convoying, temporary closures, and slower transit schedules, reducing effective daily throughput capacity.

An increased deployed military footprint elevates geopolitical risk and triggers a safe‑haven bid for long-dated sovereign bonds (especially US Treasuries), putting downward pressure on long-term yields.

A sustained increase in U.S. and allied force deployments to the Middle East prompts the redeployment of NATO/US air, naval and ISR assets away from Europe, reducing the deterrence and targeting support available to Ukraine and thereby enabling Russia to raise the tempo of offensive strikes.

Sharp escalations and visible use of commercially sourced dual‑use technologies (drones, comms, EW) prompt rapid policy responses (export controls, investment screening) and political pressure to harderen tech decoupling between the US and strategic competitors, raising geopolitical technology tension.

Higher rates of offensive strikes (missiles, drones, naval gunfire) near coastlines and ports directly increase the number and severity of attacks, near-misses and damage events affecting ships and sea lanes.

Sudden increases in strike intensity produce acute geopolitical uncertainty and rapid portfolio reallocation (flight-to-safety, stop-losses, hedging) that raises realized volatility in global sovereign bond markets.

A sustained increase in Russian offensive attacks compels the US and NATO to redeploy naval, air and ground assets to Europe for deterrence and reinforcement, reducing the scale of forces and platforms the US can keep deployed in the Middle East vis-à-vis Iran.

Higher combat intensity in Ukraine drives accelerated US transfers of precision munitions and long‑range strike ordnance to Ukraine, depleting stocks and constraining the tempo at which the US can initiate offensive strikes against Iranian targets.

Increased vulnerability of terminals, pipelines and loading facilities raises the likelihood of damage or precautionary shutdowns at key chokepoint terminals, directly lowering physical daily throughput capacity through those sea lanes.

Damage or credible threat to energy infrastructure weakens the currencies of affected energy-exporting or energy-dependent countries, prompting central banks to sell reserves or conduct outright FX operations to stabilize exchange rates.

Lowered exports of gas and liquid fuels to importing regions cause power shortages or higher electricity prices that force data-center curtailments or delay new AI cluster deployments, reducing deployable compute capacity in affected markets.

Reductions in the volume of exported oil and LNG visible to markets tighten near-term supply expectations and elevate geopolitical supply-risk premia, while increases in throughput suppress immediate risk perceptions.
A sustained drop in energy exports tightens global energy supply, lifts inflation and risk premia expectations, and drives investors to demand higher yields on long-dated sovereign debt.

A drop in Russian energy exports pushes global energy prices upward, increasing economic and political costs of further supply shocks and making US decision‑makers less willing to authorize strikes on Iran that could aggravate energy market disruptions.

Cross-border incidents and near-border escalations increase perceived security risk among governments and institutional investors, triggering accelerated defense procurement and venture/private capital directed into AI surveillance, autonomy and resilience projects.

Rising cross-border incidents increase risks of capital flight and banking stress, causing central banks to implement ad hoc controls or politically-driven policy moves that undermine markets' confidence in their commitment to stated objectives.

Sanctions, port closures and insurance/route disruptions tied to the war constrain shipments of critical feedstocks and specialty gases (e.g., neon, helium, palladium) and delay equipment deliveries to fabs, directly reducing semiconductor manufacturing throughput.

Expanded sanctions, port bans, transit restrictions and insurance limitations force tankers to idle, reflag, or avoid routes through contested areas, reducing the effective commercial tanker supply available for chokepoint-related trades.

Sustained acceleration in AI compute demand prompts corporate and public investment in data centers and fabs financed by long‑dated issuance, increasing supply of longer‑term debt and pushing up long‑term yields over the investment cycle.

Higher semiconductor manufacturing throughput increases availability of industrial-control and power-electronics chips on global and secondary markets, enabling repair, replacement and upkeep of pipeline/compression and LNG control systems and thus sustaining or raising Russian energy export flows.

Large, rapid reallocations of capital into AI projects drive leveraged positioning and periodic funding/withdrawal cycles that force cross‑asset rebalancing and margin calls, spilling over into increased volatility in the bond market.

A sustained rise in investment into AI startups and applied AI systems speeds production and export of AI-enabled ISR/targeting packages (by allied firms or contractors) that Ukraine can integrate, increasing the tempo and precision of offensive strikes.

Escalating US–China technology confrontation prompts more state and paramilitary deployments, interdictions and harassment around strategic sea lanes (to signal resolve, protect undersea infrastructure or retaliate), directly increasing the frequency and severity of maritime security incidents.

Technology‑related sanctions, export controls and insurance restrictions tied to the US–China rivalry cause operators and insurers to avoid certain flags, ports and routes, forcing longer voyages, detentions or idling that reduce effective tanker tonnage available for commercial employment in key chokepoints.

Spikes in geopolitical technology tension (export controls, sanctions, trade restrictions) create acute cross‑border capital and trade flows that prompt authorities to buy or sell FX to stabilize strategic exchange rates and secure supply chains.
Heightened technology geopolitics increases risk‑off demand for safe‑haven sovereign debt, raising prices and thereby lowering long‑term bond yields in the near term.

Escalating US–China tech confrontation drives China to deepen trade, investment and sanctions‑evasion ties with Iran (tech transfers, financial channels), provoking US diplomatic protests, sanctions and reciprocal measures that raise bilateral diplomatic tension with Iran.

Reductions in physical transit capacity through key chokepoints delay or block delivery of critical semiconductor inputs and heavy fab equipment, forcing fabs to slow or suspend production and lowering effective chip production throughput.

Physical reductions or closures of key straits (e.g., minefields, port closures, or convoy restrictions) directly limit the number of tankers and LNG carriers that can transit, immediately lowering seaborne energy export volumes from Black Sea/adjacent Russian terminals.

A decline in chokepoint throughput (closures or capacity losses) provokes immediate diplomatic escalation by the US — public condemnations, sanctions pressure and regional consultations — raising bilateral and multilateral tensions with parties seen as responsible or obstructive.

Material declines in seaborne oil/LNG shipments constrain fuel availability or raise prices for power generation in import-dependent markets, causing utilities or data center operators to curtail operations or postpone deployments and thus reducing available compute capacity.
A sustained rise in seaborne hydrocarbon flows eases energy supply pressures and inflation expectations and reduces term premia, thereby lowering long-dated sovereign bond yields.

Loss of available tanker tonnage (from reflagging problems, sanctions, or crews refusing voyages) reduces the effective shipping capacity available to move Russian and regional hydrocarbons, directly cutting export throughput until tonnage is repositioned.

A sharp uptick in hostile or disruptive maritime incidents (attacks, seizures) immediately triggers defensive policy responses (sanctions, export controls, reciprocal tech restrictions) and accelerated decoupling steps that raise geopolitical technology tension between China and the US.

Spikes in maritime security incidents create sudden supply and geopolitical uncertainty that trigger rapid portfolio reallocation and flight-to-quality moves, producing sharp, immediate increases in realized volatility in sovereign bond markets.

Higher frequency/severity of incidents disrupts export receipts and amplifies exchange-rate swings for exposed currencies, prompting authorities to step into FX markets with purchases or sales to smooth volatility and defend exchange-rate targets.

Attacks, seizures, or mine incidents on commercial vessels provoke coastal states, ports, and insurers to impose routing bans, naval escorts, and formal/informal port restrictions, thereby increasing trade and transport constraints for goods tied to the conflict zone.

Hostile or accidental maritime incidents in or near contested waters increase the likelihood of cross-border naval engagements, interdictions, or diplomatic/military responses by neighboring states, raising the rate of regional spillover incidents.
A rise in hostile or disruptive incidents against commercial ships prompts rapid redeployments of US naval and air assets for escorts, patrols and deterrence in the affected sea lanes.

When attacks on shipping are attributed to Iranian forces or their proxies, US or allied commanders frequently respond with targeted kinetic strikes against perpetrators or their infrastructure, increasing retaliatory strike frequency.

Elevated market perception of maritime supply‑chain risk raises investor risk premia and prompts lenders and VCs to pull back financing for capital‑intensive AI infrastructure and projects—especially those sited in or dependent on exposed trade corridors—reducing capital flows to AI.
An increase in market risk perception raises risk premia and accelerates forced and discretionary portfolio rebalancing, directly increasing intraday and realized volatility in bond markets.

Sharp increases in market-perceived risk and energy-price volatility create political and economic pressure on US decision‑makers to authorize offensive actions aimed at securing supply routes or deterring further disruptions.

Sustained rises in long-term yields increase the cost of financing large-scale data-center and accelerator deployments and reduce corporate capex appetite, slowing the growth rate of demand for high-performance AI compute.

Rising long-term sovereign yields increase ship financing and leasing costs and encourage owners to idle, cancel newbuilds or defer deployment, reducing effective tanker tonnage available for commercial employment.

Sustained increases in global long-term yields raise sovereign borrowing costs and debt-service burdens for Western governments, eroding short-to-medium-term fiscal headroom and thereby slowing or reducing external military assistance and munitions supply to Ukraine, which lowers the pace and scale of offensive operations.

Rising long-term sovereign yields raise US fiscal financing costs and political scrutiny over deficit spending, shifting executive focus toward domestic economic management and making leaders less willing to authorize new offensive strikes that would carry budgetary and political costs.

Spikes in bond-market volatility increase market-wide risk aversion and trigger redemptions and value-at-risk driven de-risking by funds, reducing new equity and debt allocations into AI projects and infrastructure.

Sharp increases in bond-market volatility drive broad investor risk aversion and repricing, directly raising market participants' perception of geopolitical and supply-disruption risk that is applied to maritime energy exposure.

Sharp spikes in bond-market volatility tighten trade finance and commodity lending lines and push up insurance and margin requirements for energy shipments, producing delays, cancellations or reduced volumes of cross-border energy exports from Russia and Ukraine.

Acute bond-market volatility produces risk-off shocks that threaten energy and shipping markets and investor confidence, prompting the US to surge naval and air assets to the Gulf and nearby sea lanes to deter disruptions and reassure markets and partners.

A significant depreciation of a major chip-producing country's currency versus currencies used to invoice fab equipment and imported materials raises local costs for capacity expansion, delaying or shrinking planned production ramp-ups.

A depreciation of a major hydrocarbon-importing currency versus the invoice currency (i.e., an increase in the bilateral exchange rate) raises local import costs and leads importers to reduce or delay seaborne oil/LNG purchases, lowering physical flows.

A marked loss of central bank credibility raises risk premia and investor uncertainty, increasing borrowing costs and prompting institutional and VC investors to pull back or delay new commitments to AI startups and infrastructure.

Strike authorization propensity
nodes.description: The degree to which executive decision-makers are inclined to authorize offensive military strikes.

nodes.label: Offensive strike rate
nodes.description: The frequency of initiated kinetic or armed strike operations per unit time in the theater.

nodes.label: Retaliatory strike rate
nodes.description: The rate at which counter- or retaliatory armed responses occur after an initial attack.

nodes.label: Ally restraint pressure
nodes.description: The level of political and diplomatic pressure from regional partners urging restraint or de-escalation.

nodes.label: Diplomatic tension level
nodes.description: The overall intensity of diplomatic hostility and strain between the conflicting sides and their partners.

nodes.label: Embassy and consular risk level
nodes.description: The assessed threat to diplomatic posts and consular operations in the region.

nodes.label: Energy market volatility
nodes.description: The short‑term variability in energy prices and market indicators linked to regional security developments.

nodes.label: Risk to energy infrastructure
nodes.description: The probability and intent of attacks or disruptions targeting energy production, transport, or storage assets.

nodes.label: Military presence level
nodes.description: The aggregate scale of deployed military forces and platforms operating in the theater.

nodes.label: Munitions and matériel stockpile
nodes.description: The on‑hand quantity of weapons, munitions, and strike-capable matériel available to forces in the region.

nodes.label: Intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance coverage
nodes.description: The extent and persistence of ISR assets providing situational awareness across the operational area.

nodes.label: Travel advisory intensity
nodes.description: The severity and prevalence of official travel warnings and evacuation advisories issued for the region.

nodes.label: Economic coercion level
nodes.description: The strength and scope of economic pressure measures such as sanctions, tariffs, or trade restrictions.

nodes.label: Cyber-attack activity rate
nodes.description: The frequency of offensive cyber operations and disruptive intrusions related to the confrontation.

nodes.label: Diplomatic engagement intensity
nodes.description: The degree of active negotiation, back‑channel diplomacy, and mediated contacts aimed at managing the dispute.

nodes.label: Domestic political support for force
nodes.description: The level of public and elite domestic backing for the use of military force or escalation.

nodes.label: Energy infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: Susceptibility of energy production, processing and distribution assets to damage or disruption.

nodes.label: Energy export throughput

nodes.label: Sanctions enforcement coherence
nodes.description: Degree of alignment and consistent application among sanctioning actors and mechanisms.

nodes.label: Political support for external aid
nodes.description: Level of domestic political backing for providing military, economic or humanitarian assistance to conflict parties.

nodes.label: Diplomatic tension level
nodes.description: Intensity of diplomatic strain and hostile interactions across bilateral and multilateral relationships in the region.

nodes.label: Regional spillover incident rate
nodes.description: Frequency of cross-border or neighboring-state incidents (incursions, accidents, diplomatic breaches) per unit time.

nodes.label: Energy market price volatility
nodes.description: Magnitude and frequency of short-term fluctuations in global energy and fuel prices.

nodes.label: Civilian casualty rate
nodes.description: Number of civilian fatalities and serious injuries caused by hostilities per unit time.

nodes.label: Displaced population stock
nodes.description: Total number of internally displaced persons and refugees resulting from the conflict at a given time.

nodes.label: Logistics resilience
nodes.description: Capacity of transport, storage and supply networks to sustain movement of goods and military supplies under stress.

nodes.label: Defense procurement rate
nodes.description: Pace at which military equipment, munitions and support systems are ordered, delivered and integrated per unit time.

nodes.label: Information warfare intensity
nodes.description: Scale and aggressiveness of propaganda, misinformation and information operations aimed at domestic and external audiences.

nodes.label: Trade and transport restriction level
nodes.description: Degree of formal and informal constraints on trade, shipping and transit affecting commodity flows and logistics.

AI compute demand growth
nodes.description: The rate at which global demand for high-performance compute for AI training and inference is increasing or decreasing.

nodes.label: Available compute capacity
nodes.description: The total deployable compute resource pool (accelerators, servers, clusters) available for AI workloads at a point in time.

nodes.label: Data‑center buildout rate
nodes.description: The pace at which new data‑center floor space and server infrastructure are being planned, financed, and brought online.

nodes.label: Power and infrastructure stress
nodes.description: The degree to which electricity generation, distribution, cooling, and related infrastructure are strained by incremental compute and data‑center loads.

nodes.label: Chip production capacity
nodes.description: The available manufacturing throughput for AI‑relevant semiconductors and packaging across the global fabrication ecosystem.

nodes.label: Memory and component price level
nodes.description: The prevailing price level for memory modules and other critical components used in AI hardware, expressed as a continuously varying index.

nodes.label: Capital flow to AI projects
nodes.description: The rate and volume of new financial investment (equity, debt, project finance) directed toward AI infrastructure, startups, and deployments.

nodes.label: Credit market stress
nodes.description: The level of borrowing cost, liquidity tightness, and risk premia that affect financing availability for large AI investments.

nodes.label: Investment concentration
nodes.description: The degree to which AI investment and compute capacity are concentrated among a small number of projects, regions, or platforms.

nodes.label: AI safety incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency at which deployed or tested AI systems produce harmful, uncontrolled, or clearly unsafe outcomes per unit time or per test volume.

nodes.label: Agent autonomy level
nodes.description: The average degree of independent decision‑making and action capability built into deployed AI agents and automated systems.

nodes.label: Cybersecurity breach rate
nodes.description: The rate at which AI systems, development environments, or associated infrastructure experience successful cyber intrusions or unauthorized access.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny intensity
nodes.description: The intensity and scope of regulatory attention, enforcement actions, and compliance obligations directed at AI development and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Geopolitical technology tension
nodes.description: The level of strategic friction and policy countermeasures in the international system specifically tied to technology, trade, and supply‑chain policy.

nodes.label: Supply‑chain bottleneck level
nodes.description: The aggregated severity of bottlenecks across logistics, component supply, and manufacturing lead times affecting AI hardware and buildouts.

nodes.label: Skilled AI talent supply
nodes.description: The available pool of experienced engineers, researchers, and technical staff capable of building, operating, and securing advanced AI systems.

Chokepoint transit capacity
nodes.description: The aggregate physical throughput capacity (ships/day or barrels/day equivalent) available through key maritime chokepoints used by hydrocarbon shipping.

nodes.label: Seaborne hydrocarbon flow
nodes.description: The volume rate of oil and LNG moved by sea across the system (barrels or tons per time unit).

nodes.label: Tanker fleet availability
nodes.description: The active supply of tanker tonnage available for commercial employment and rerouting (effective fleet utilization and idle capacity).

nodes.label: Tanker freight rates
nodes.description: Market freight rates and time-charter levels for crude and product tankers that determine shipping cost per unit transported.

nodes.label: Shipping insurance premiums
nodes.description: The average cost level of war, hull, and cargo insurance for maritime hydrocarbon shipments, expressed as premium rates.

nodes.label: Maritime security incidents
nodes.description: The frequency and severity of hostile or disruptive incidents affecting ships and sea lanes (attacks, seizures, near-misses) per time unit.

nodes.label: Upstream production output
nodes.description: The rate of hydrocarbon production from upstream sources (crude oil and gas liquids and feedstock gas) available for export or domestic processing.

nodes.label: Producer coordination intensity
nodes.description: The degree and effectiveness of coordinated production/policy actions among supplying actors that influence aggregate output decisions.

nodes.label: Refining throughput and margins
nodes.description: Aggregate refinery processing rates and the associated refining margin spreads that determine conversion capacity and crack economics.

nodes.label: Spot crude price level
nodes.description: The prevailing short-term market price level for benchmark crude oils in physical spot markets.

nodes.label: Spot LNG price level
nodes.description: The prevailing short-term market price level for LNG cargoes in spot markets.

nodes.label: Futures market volatility
nodes.description: The volatility (realized or implied) in hydrocarbon derivatives markets reflecting uncertainty about future prices.

nodes.label: Trader and commercial inventory levels
nodes.description: The volume of commercial oil and LNG stocks held by traders, refiners, and merchants available to smooth shortfalls.

nodes.label: Shipping rerouting cost
nodes.description: The additional distance, time and operational cost per shipment arising from detours to avoid risky or closed sea lanes.

nodes.label: Maritime finance liquidity
nodes.description: The availability and terms of debt and working capital for shipowners and charterers to finance vessel operations and chartering.

nodes.label: Market risk perception
nodes.description: The prevailing collective perception of geopolitical and supply disruption risk among market participants influencing behaviour and pricing premia.

Policy rate level
nodes.description: The prevailing short-term policy interest rate set by monetary authorities.

nodes.label: Long-term bond yield
nodes.description: The yield on long-dated sovereign bonds reflecting long-term borrowing costs.

nodes.label: Yield curve slope
nodes.description: The spread between long-term and short-term interest rates indicating term premia and expectations.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Market and agent forecasts of future inflation over relevant horizons.

nodes.label: Realized inflation
nodes.description: Observed changes in consumer prices or other inflation measures over a recent period.

nodes.label: Bond market volatility
nodes.description: The variability or realized volatility of bond prices and yields.

nodes.label: FX market volatility
nodes.description: The variability or realized volatility of foreign-exchange rates and FX trading conditions.

nodes.label: Bilateral exchange rate
nodes.description: The market price of one currency expressed in units of another, measured continuously.

nodes.label: Official FX intervention
nodes.description: The rate, direction and magnitude of official purchases or sales of currency in the FX market.

nodes.label: Net capital flows
nodes.description: Cross-border private and portfolio capital movements into or out of a market or economy.

nodes.label: Foreign-exchange reserves
nodes.description: The stock of official foreign assets available to support exchange-rate and liquidity operations.

nodes.label: Market liquidity
nodes.description: The ease with which large positions can be transacted without materially moving prices.

nodes.label: Funding costs
nodes.description: The prevailing costs of short- and medium-term wholesale funding for market participants.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: The aggregate willingness of investors to hold riskier assets versus safe assets.

nodes.label: Policy communication clarity
nodes.description: The clarity and predictability of authorities' public communications about future policy.

nodes.label: Central bank credibility
nodes.description: The market's confidence that monetary authorities will achieve stated policy objectives.

A sustained rise in seaborne hydrocarbon flows eases energy supply pressures and inflation expectations and reduces term premia, thereby lowering long-dated sovereign bond yields.

Loss of available tanker tonnage (from reflagging problems, sanctions, or crews refusing voyages) reduces the effective shipping capacity available to move Russian and regional hydrocarbons, directly cutting export throughput until tonnage is repositioned.

A sharp uptick in hostile or disruptive maritime incidents (attacks, seizures) immediately triggers defensive policy responses (sanctions, export controls, reciprocal tech restrictions) and accelerated decoupling steps that raise geopolitical technology tension between China and the US.

Spikes in maritime security incidents create sudden supply and geopolitical uncertainty that trigger rapid portfolio reallocation and flight-to-quality moves, producing sharp, immediate increases in realized volatility in sovereign bond markets.

Higher frequency/severity of incidents disrupts export receipts and amplifies exchange-rate swings for exposed currencies, prompting authorities to step into FX markets with purchases or sales to smooth volatility and defend exchange-rate targets.

Attacks, seizures, or mine incidents on commercial vessels provoke coastal states, ports, and insurers to impose routing bans, naval escorts, and formal/informal port restrictions, thereby increasing trade and transport constraints for goods tied to the conflict zone.

Hostile or accidental maritime incidents in or near contested waters increase the likelihood of cross-border naval engagements, interdictions, or diplomatic/military responses by neighboring states, raising the rate of regional spillover incidents.
A rise in hostile or disruptive incidents against commercial ships prompts rapid redeployments of US naval and air assets for escorts, patrols and deterrence in the affected sea lanes.

When attacks on shipping are attributed to Iranian forces or their proxies, US or allied commanders frequently respond with targeted kinetic strikes against perpetrators or their infrastructure, increasing retaliatory strike frequency.

Elevated market perception of maritime supply‑chain risk raises investor risk premia and prompts lenders and VCs to pull back financing for capital‑intensive AI infrastructure and projects—especially those sited in or dependent on exposed trade corridors—reducing capital flows to AI.
An increase in market risk perception raises risk premia and accelerates forced and discretionary portfolio rebalancing, directly increasing intraday and realized volatility in bond markets.

Sharp increases in market-perceived risk and energy-price volatility create political and economic pressure on US decision‑makers to authorize offensive actions aimed at securing supply routes or deterring further disruptions.

Sustained rises in long-term yields increase the cost of financing large-scale data-center and accelerator deployments and reduce corporate capex appetite, slowing the growth rate of demand for high-performance AI compute.

Rising long-term sovereign yields increase ship financing and leasing costs and encourage owners to idle, cancel newbuilds or defer deployment, reducing effective tanker tonnage available for commercial employment.

Sustained increases in global long-term yields raise sovereign borrowing costs and debt-service burdens for Western governments, eroding short-to-medium-term fiscal headroom and thereby slowing or reducing external military assistance and munitions supply to Ukraine, which lowers the pace and scale of offensive operations.

Rising long-term sovereign yields raise US fiscal financing costs and political scrutiny over deficit spending, shifting executive focus toward domestic economic management and making leaders less willing to authorize new offensive strikes that would carry budgetary and political costs.

Spikes in bond-market volatility increase market-wide risk aversion and trigger redemptions and value-at-risk driven de-risking by funds, reducing new equity and debt allocations into AI projects and infrastructure.

Sharp increases in bond-market volatility drive broad investor risk aversion and repricing, directly raising market participants' perception of geopolitical and supply-disruption risk that is applied to maritime energy exposure.

Sharp spikes in bond-market volatility tighten trade finance and commodity lending lines and push up insurance and margin requirements for energy shipments, producing delays, cancellations or reduced volumes of cross-border energy exports from Russia and Ukraine.

Acute bond-market volatility produces risk-off shocks that threaten energy and shipping markets and investor confidence, prompting the US to surge naval and air assets to the Gulf and nearby sea lanes to deter disruptions and reassure markets and partners.

A significant depreciation of a major chip-producing country's currency versus currencies used to invoice fab equipment and imported materials raises local costs for capacity expansion, delaying or shrinking planned production ramp-ups.

A depreciation of a major hydrocarbon-importing currency versus the invoice currency (i.e., an increase in the bilateral exchange rate) raises local import costs and leads importers to reduce or delay seaborne oil/LNG purchases, lowering physical flows.

A marked loss of central bank credibility raises risk premia and investor uncertainty, increasing borrowing costs and prompting institutional and VC investors to pull back or delay new commitments to AI startups and infrastructure.
